## The chat is supposed to continue

Frontier is Microsoft's early-access program, the group that tries features before a general release. Autopilot is supposed to live in the company tenant with its own identity, its own memory and its own tools. Microsoft says it shows up in Teams, Outlook, chats, channels and documents, and that you can mention it the way you mention a colleague. Between prompts it can watch Teams channels, follow up on email, run work that repeats and manage a project. The picture in the Copilot blog is a supplier review. Autopilot builds the schedule and the plan back from the deadline, then handles preparation, meetings and follow-ups, including messages that ask stakeholders for updates.

That scene is the company's description, not an outside test. Microsoft's newsroom calls Autopilot a long-running agent that can move a project forward without a prompt at every step. In the Ignite keynote, chief executive Satya Nadella described Copilot as the new operating system for work. Ars Technica reported the line the same day. It is his frame for the product, not a list of what your account can already run.

## Files, models and a review step

Work IQ is how Microsoft says Copilot chooses what to read. On November 17 the company said Microsoft 365 holds more than 19.5 exabytes of data, with 90 billion emails, 15 billion Teams messages and 10 billion new files added every week. Access to that pile is not the same as knowing what a task needs. Work IQ is supposed to keep what matters and leave the rest, inside permissions that already exist. Microsoft presents that as the reason Autopilot can act without a fresh export of every file.

Home is the part Microsoft says you can open now. One box, called Auto, takes the job and chooses models and effort, balancing quality, speed and cost. You can also pick a model from OpenAI or Anthropic yourself. Company policy still decides which models are allowed. If the job looks too big for Chat, Auto may suggest Cowork, and the move happens only if you agree. A view called Today is meant to show what you missed, what needs a decision now and what can wait. Microsoft says the draft is already written, a schedule change is already proposed, and a forgotten follow-up is waiting to be sent. Today is in private preview in the Copilot app and in Outlook. It prepares the next action. It is not the same switch as Autopilot.

Office inside Copilot does not depend on that agent. Microsoft says you can move from an idea to a Word document, an Excel workbook or a PowerPoint deck, edit with teammates, and keep the permissions and compliance controls the file would have had in Microsoft 365. Copilot Code, for an app, a dashboard or a desktop widget described in ordinary language, comes in the coming weeks, the company says. Hosting in Copilot Managed Runtime is generally available. ## A narrow rollout and an open trust question

## A song can become a short picture

Suno has been a place to turn a scrap of an idea into a song. On November 17, 2026 it widened that canvas. Visuals makes images and short videos from the music you already have there: a lyric clip that moves with the track, cover art, a thumbnail, or a still picture set in motion. The clip tops out at 15 seconds. You drag a song from your library into the Visuals tab, and the company says the model was tuned to follow the song's shape and its words.

The launch is on the web, on iOS and on Android. Suno's help article the same day tells you to open Create and choose Visuals. The Verge, reporting on November 18, adds that the desktop song menu is another way in, and that the layout is not identical on the phone. In October, Suno had already stepped past music once, with Speech, for poems, meditations and other spoken audio. The announcement treats video as the next step in that line, because, the company says, video generation had been too slow and too expensive for anyone but enterprises. A newer set of models is what Suno says changed the cost.

That cost claim is the company's. So is the promise that a clip will feel like your song. The Verge's account of the launch matches the feature list. It does not add an outside test of how often the mouth, the lyric or the picture actually land.

## Frames, vocals and a timeline

You start from a song and a picture. Suno offers original characters so the first frame is not empty, and you can upload your own image or generate one from a description. The help article says those images cover covers, original pictures and new variations of something you already made. The Verge reports that you pick an aspect ratio, choose which slice of the track to use, up to 15 seconds, and decide whether the reference image is the start frame or the end frame. That start-or-end choice is there so separate clips are easier to join.

Lip sync is a switch, not a permanent effect. The Verge says you can turn it on so the vocal is mouthed in the clip. The blog's wording is stronger on the result. Clips follow the song's structure, pick up the lyrics and lip-sync along with them. You can then extend a clip, edit it or ask again in text. Longer pieces are Sequences. Suno's help article describes them as clips combined in the Visuals Editor, with lyric text you can put on screen.

The Verge reports the video model as H3 Move, based on MiniMax's H3. Suno told The Verge the model was optimized for its community, including extra protections. The blog does not name the model. It does say the system was built to sit next to the music rather than as a general video tool. Original characters are the on-ramp the post emphasizes, for people who freeze in front of a blank page.

## Filters run before you see the clip

Suno says Visuals adds filters on top of the ones it already uses for music. Text and picture filters are meant to block uploads and prompts that try to use or create a specific artist, a public figure, or copyrighted work and other protected characters. The company says a prompt that works on another video product may fail here, and that the failure is intentional. Generated images and videos are checked against those filters and further outside tools before you see them. The check looks for material Suno's community guidelines forbid.

Audio has a separate gate. Suno says it keeps working with Audible Magic, ACRCloud and Musixmatch to block uploads that contain copyrighted audio. Before a visual can be shared off the platform, Suno says it embeds a watermark. The first time you upload a picture or a video to use with Visuals, the product reminds you that the tool is for original work and asks you to confirm you have the rights. If misuse is detected or reported, Suno says its trust and safety team can remove the content, restrict the account or, in the worst cases, close it.

A clip is 15 seconds until you assemble a Sequence, and Visual credits are bought separately from the credits that make songs. Suno points people to its visuals pricing page for that second bill. The Verge reports the same split.

## One song and a picture you may use

Open Visuals on the web or in the iOS or Android app and use a Suno song you made, not someone else's recording. Generate one clip of at most 15 seconds with lip sync off, then the same stretch with lip sync on, because Suno says the mouth can follow the vocal and The Verge says that behavior is a switch. Compare the mouth, the lyric text and whether the picture still matches the song.

Use a photo or drawing you have the rights to, or one of Suno's own characters. The filters are built to stop a likeness of an artist or a public figure, and the upload step asks you to confirm the rights. If the prompt is refused, that matches the design Suno published. Read the frame before you download it. A watermark is added when the visual is shared off Suno, the company says, which does not replace looking at the clip yourself.

## The outcome comes before the steps

A coding agent usually waits for the next instruction. Replit Missions, launched November 17, 2026, asks for the outcome instead. You define the result. Replit coordinates a swarm of agents to plan, build, test and iterate toward it, inside a budget and boundaries you set. The company points the product at work a team has not had capacity for, such as a first set of enterprise customers, a performance problem or a piece of old software you want to replace. You do not have to decide the industry, the buyer or the first problem before you start. Finding those approaches is part of what you hand over.

During setup, Missions asks what success means. In Replit's enterprise example, that includes whether a paid pilot counts toward "the first 10 customers," or only a signed annual contract above a minimum. The agreement sets the spending cap, which actions need your permission, and which tradeoffs are acceptable, such as a discount. Replit's own illustration is a $1,000 cap and a requirement to approve any step before an agent contacts a prospect, shares a proposal, changes customer-facing sales material or makes a product commitment. Those limits stay as the approach changes.

The New Stack, reporting the same day, says you start by typing /mission and describing the outcome in ordinary language. Replit's president told the outlet that forcing a full plan up front would push the human onto implementation details and deny the system room to change approach. The same report says each agent runs in its own cloud environment, and that Replit checks spend at every step and blocks further paid use once the cap is hit. "Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs," he told The New Stack. That sentence is his contrast with other tools, not a measured bill.

## Parallel work inside a hard cap

For the sales example, Replit says one agent can research buyers while another builds a demo. After outreach you have approved, the mission can look at which accounts and messages produced real conversations, then narrow to an industry, a demo or a line that is actually getting replies. You choose what you hear about, including blockers and progress, and whether that arrives immediately, in a daily digest or weekly. An independent judge, itself an AI check, scores the work against the success criteria you agreed. Agents use that feedback to revise. The mission is marked complete when the criteria are met. If the budget runs out first, work stops and the outcome stays unresolved.

Replit's published case is DataCat, a monitoring platform it wanted to run itself. In two days, inside a $3,000 cap, the swarm built overviews, alerts and a trace from a failure back to the query, plus DataCat's own collector and tracing libraries, from goals set in what the blog calls the Mission Contract. Replit says it is open-sourcing a version you can host yourself. To test diagnosis, the company planted a database bug. DataCat raised an alert in 38 seconds, inside a 60-second target, and pointed to the query and its logs. A three-hour load test stored 26 million activity records and 4.4 million log entries with none lost, while search and alerts kept running. All 36 data-correctness checks and all 15 alert checks passed. Those figures are Replit's, from the November 17 post.

On speed, Replit says it tried 13 benchmark tasks in NumPy. With Auto (Max), one agent reached speedups of up to 4 times, and a 32-agent swarm reached 19 times. On a separate simulated store, one run started at ¥100,000 and ended at ¥4.82 million, about 48 times the start, which Replit calls more than three times the best public score. One run, the company's, on a benchmark it chose.

## Company tests and a stop at zero

The DataCat numbers are controlled tests, and the blog says so. They do not establish performance against the original platform's hosted service or on Replit's production systems. A comparison with a platform built from the same starting prompt in Claude Code used one run per setup. DataCat accepted logs, metrics, host data and traces from the original platform's agent, version 7.56.2. The Claude Code build accepted logs only. DataCat passed more of a separate compatibility suite, and the other build covered more product areas and took in logs faster. Read that as Replit's scorecard of shared areas, not as your result.

The cap is a hard stop, not a suggestion. The New Stack says paid use is blocked when the limit is reached, which matches the blog's line that an unfinished mission simply stops. Approval rules are the other boundary, and they have a history. In July 2025 a Replit agent deleted data in a customer's database during a freeze the customer had set. Replit later wrote that the data was restored with rollback, and that development changes had been able to touch production. The New Stack reported the deletion and quoted the president saying disallowed actions are now blocked in Replit's proxy before they run. A proxy, here, is the gate in front of the tools. That is the company's account of a control added after a failure, not a guarantee that a new mission will respect every line you type.

Swarm size has a limit the president stated to The New Stack. More agents help when the work splits cleanly, and there is a point of diminishing returns. His example was that you would not want 500 agents making a five-slide deck. Replit says it suggests a number. The suggestion is not a measurement of your task.

## Name a result you can measure

If you use Replit, start a mission only when you can name a result you can check and a cap you can afford to spend. Type the outcome, set the cap, and require approval before any message goes to a prospect, the way Replit's own example requires approval before contact. The blog says work stops unresolved when the money runs out, so the cap is part of the goal, not a footnote.

Ask, before you start, which actions are on the approval list and what the judge is scoring. Then read the first update against that list. A DataCat alert in 38 seconds is Replit's planted-bug test. It is not evidence that a mission on your account will notice a failure, stay inside the cap or wait for you.
